items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Well the Jelly Roll Morton album for Columbia was Sam Parkins’ idea... that perhaps Jelly Roll Morton would be the next on the list and that’s why we did that album.

ctx.x: Well the Jelly Roll Morton album for Columbia was Sam Parkins’ idea, the producer. And he thought, and he got Columbia to think, that with the unexpected popularity of Scott Joplin from the movie “The Sting” and the various recordings, including my own, that perhaps Jelly Roll Morton would be the next on the list and that’s why we did that album. And we did it with several components. We did it like that record of “Grandpa’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

Spells” like that track of “Grandpa’s Spells” with a big band. It was my idea to make it like to a big concert marching band and that’s the way I arranged those things. We also did some smaller bands and we also did a couple of things as a trio with Joe Venuti — Panama Francis and Venuti and I. In fact Jelly Roll Morton did not become the next pop hit after Scott Joplin and I think the record has never paid for itself.

items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: The records included stuff by Jelly Roll Morton... I brushed off what I remembered from all that and got involved in Scott Joplin specifically and Jelly Roll Morton

ctx.x: Well I’ve noticed that one thing that we’ve been interested in here in doing these archival tapes is that we keep some of the earlier jazz stories and music alive for students and anyone watching. And it seems to be kind of a passion of yours that the early, some of the early keyboard styles. Is this something that you’ve liked from the beginning? Or did you come to it later on?

I liked it from the beginning, and the beginning for me really was a large collection of 78 RPM records which my big brother had collected and left to me when he went off to college. That really was my basic education. The records included stuff by Jelly Roll © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Morton, stuff by Fats Waller and Teddy Wilson. And although I didn’t like it much at first, even stuff by Zez Confrey and ragtime people like that, novelty piano people like that. But I never thought that I would be using that background in my professional career. It never seemed that there was any reason to expect that.
